Thursday-Monday: Several Pacific storm systems will impact the 
PacNW into early next week. The first arrives today (Thursday), 
followed by a second on Friday, then third Sunday into Monday. 
Widespread precipitation will accompany Thursday and Sunday into 
Monday. Friday will be more localized to areas of southern WA and 
the lower Idaho Panhandle. Much of the precipitation will fall as 
rain in the lowlands with any moisture through Friday. Snow will 
mainly be found in the higher elevations above 5000 feet with 
minor deviations. The system on Sunday will be a bit more complex 
with precip-type. If you are looking for breaks in the 
precipitation, Friday will be a top candidate for many areas of WA
and North Idaho and then for much of the region on Saturday. 

Thanksgiving: Satellite reveals a deep low churning off the BC 
Coast steering a plume of subtropical moisture into the region. 
Moderate precipitation has reached NW WA with lighter activity 
filling in over the Cascades and northern Washington. 
Precipitation will continue to fill in across the Inland NW 
through the morning hours with light to moderate rates. A midlevel
shortwave will eject inland Thursday morning and push a cold 
front through the region crossing through Central WA 6-8AM, 
Eastern WA 10-12PM, and slowly sagging through Idaho and far 
southeastern WA 12-3PM. The heaviest precipitation will fall ahead
of the cold front. Precipitation in the lee of the Cascades and 
across the Basin will end once the front passes through but 
orographic showers will pick back along the Cascade Crest and into
the rising terrain of NE WA and N ID as gusty southwest winds 
develop. Moderate QPF amounts 0.25-0.75 inches are forecast for 
the northern tier of Idaho and Washington with amounts between a 
0.10-0.20 inches into the lower Basin. Heavier amounts closer to 
an inch are expected for the Cascade Crest and higher peaks of the
Idaho Panhandle. 

Snow impacts: Washington Pass is currently 26F and confidence is 
high for heavy snow leading to very challenging travel. Winter 
storm warnings are in place for this Cascade Pass. Sherman Pass 
will also receive snow but confidence remains low for moderate or 
higher impacts. Temperatures are currently at 32F with snow just 
starting. With warm air advection, this will be a heavy wet snow 
and the 3 inches in the forecast seems reasonable but if 
temperatures can hold near 32F, amounts cloud be closer to 5-7 
inches. Temperatures remain well above freezing in the upper 
Methow Valley suggesting rain vs snow. 

Wind: Breezy southeast winds Thursday morning will shift to the 
southwest as the cold comes through. Southwest wind speeds will 
increase across the Columbia Basin, Palouse, and Spokane Area with
speeds of 15 to 20 mph coupled with gusts 25-35 mph. There is a 
15% chance for gusts to reach 40 mph around the West Plains, South
Hill, and higher benches of the Palouse Thursday afternoon. 
Otherwise, wind gusts 30-40 mph will mainly be confined to the 
higher peaks across the Cascades and Idaho Panhandle. 

Friday: The day will start off dry with patchy fog across the 
sheltered northern valleys. 500mb heights will be rising from the 
southwest ahead of the next low crossing into the Eastern Pacific.
The axis of subtropical moisture previously shoved southward from
Thursday's cold front will lift back northward. Meanwhile, a 
compact shortwave will come across NW WA and through the INW. This
will interact with this stalled frontal boundary and moisture 
axis draped across southern WA and the lower ID and spin up a 
surface low resulting in areas of light to moderate precipitation.
Models were struggling on this feature 24 hours ago and seem to 
have come into better agreement. The main threat for precipitation
will be south of the Highway 2 corridor with the potential for 
moderate intensities focusing over southeastern WA and the lower 
Idaho Panhandle around the Blue Mountains, Palouse, L-C Valley, 
and Camas Prairie. 25th-25th percentiles vary from 0.50-1.3 
inches with local amounts in the Blue Mountains near 1.6 inches. 
Further west into the lower Columbia Basin, similar percentiles 
range from 0.25-0.60 inches. Amounts drop off considerably toward 
0.20 inches or less along I-90 and even lower to Hwy 2. The 
northern mountains will likely be north of this precipitation 
event. The exception will be Stevens Pass which will hovering near
the freezing mark and have a 70% chance to pick up 2 or more 
inches of snow. Motorists should be prepared for winter travel 
conditions if heading over Stevens Friday morning and afternoon 
with snow tapering off Friday evening.

Saturday: Confidence has increased for dry conditions to briefly 
settle into the INW Saturday as northwest flow aloft transitions 
to short wave ridging. There is likely to be areas of dense fog to
contend with, otherwise the region will get a short break from 
the wet weather.
